name: Ha
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Harjula, Lotta. 2004. Handling tone in two-level morphology: the case of Ha. Nordic Journal of African Studies 13(1): 95-102. (open access, njas.fi)
catalog_locator: p. 96, section 1 'The Ha language and the problem of the parsing tone', paragraphs 5-6
catalog_quote: In my PhD dissertation (Harjula 2004) I have analysed the tonal system of Ha as a pitch-accent system, and according to this analysis there are two types of accents, i.e. lexical and grammatical accents. On the lexical level this means that all the verbal roots fall into two tonal classes, one accented and the other accent-less. For the other word classes the place of the accent also has to be defined in the lexicon. The lexical accents are realised as H tones on the mora with which they are lexically connected, unless they are moved or removed because of the grammatical accents. The phonetic changes are not taken into account here. The lexical accents, together with the grammatical accents or the absence of the accent, define the grammatical forms of the verbs. The verb forms are called lexical tone-keeping forms if the tonal contrast of the verbal roots is preserved, and lexical tone-neutralising forms if the possible accent of the root is deleted. In both the lexical tone-keeping and -neutralising forms there may also be grammatical accents that are realised on the prefixes, or on the first or the second syllable of the stem.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ha has no reported dynamic stress; prominence is a tonal (pitch-)accent. Verb roots are lexically accented or accent-less; for nouns and other classes the accent's position is lexically listed; grammatical (tense) accents fall on prefixes or the first/second stem syllable and may shift or delete lexical accents; every accent surfaces as a H tone on its mora. Supporting: Harjula 2006 p. 178 'the pitch accent is contrastive in Ha'; Bichwa 2018 p. 88 'Giha is a tone-accent language', accented vs unaccented stems, with an accent on the penult hopping back one syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic noun stems realise their accent on the class prefix; object prefixes attract the stem's lexical accent; index forms/connexive carry floating accents realised on the following word with augment lengthening; tone-neutralising verb forms delete the root accent (Harjula 2004: 96-100). Bichwa 2018: 88 reports 'Penultimate Back Hopping' of an accent off the penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical/grammatical accent realised tonally; statements concern words in isolation and in phrases (accent shift across word boundary with index forms). No statement about stress, intensity or phrase-final lengthening as stress; the full grammar (Harjula 2004, Koeppe) was not accessible and may add detail.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Ha of the Kigoma Region, Tanzania (Harjula's fieldwork 1997-2003 around Kasulu/Kibondo/Kigoma; Bichwa's 'Giha' = same language, glottocode haaa1252, ISO haq). Harjula notes several mutually intelligible dialects but does not restrict the accent analysis to one.

tone_statements.citation: Bichwa, Saul S. & Luinasia E. Kombe. 2017. The Tonological Study on Giha Infinitive Verbs. Kioo cha Lugha 15(1): 20-35. Dar es Salaam: Institute of Kiswahili Studies, University of Dar es Salaam. ISSN 0856-552X.
tone_statements.quote: Giha is among of the accented languages. Thus, this paper is aimed at identifying the Basic Tone Melody and describing the specific tone in the Basic Tone Melody which is associated with the accent in Giha infinitives. ... The findings show that the Basic Tone Melody for Giha verbs is Low, High, Low (LHL) and the accent is associated with the left side low tone of the Basic Tone Melody.
tone_statements.summary: Accentual (tone-accent) Bantu system: verbs carry a Basic Tone Melody LHL whose leftmost L links to the lexical/grammatical accent; surface tones derived by rule (Massamba-style accent-and-melody analysis), consistent with Harjula's pitch accent analysis listed here.

sources.note: p. 96: Ha tonal system analysed (in her 2004 dissertation/grammar) as a pitch accent system with lexical and grammatical accents; verbal roots are accented vs accent-less; for other word classes the place of the accent is defined in the lexicon; accents realised as H tones on the mora they are lexically linked to, unless moved/removed by grammatical accents. No mention of (dynamic) stress.

sources.note: First-hand autosegmental tone-accent analysis of Giha infinitives from recordings of 15 speakers. Abstract: 'Giha is among of the accented languages. Thus, this paper is aimed at identifying the Basic Tone Melody and describing the specific tone in the Basic Tone Melody which is associated with the accent in Giha infinitives. Also, this paper shows the rules which govern the tonological pattern in this language.. The findings show that the Basic Tone Melody for Giha verbs is Low, High, Low (LHL) and the accent is associated with the left side low tone of the Basic Tone Melody.' Not downloaded…

sources.note: Segmental paper (nasalization, ATR harmony, NC assimilation); tone only presupposed in passing ('associated tones', 'prosodic elements such as syllables and tones', citing Harjula 2004/2005, Bichwa & Kombe 2017). Examples (1)-(14) carry no tone marks (nasal tildes survive). Nothing on stress/accent.

tone.quote: Being part of the Bantu language family, igiHa experiences the phenomenon of assimilation within its phonological structure, impacting both the characteristics of its segments (including consonants and vowels) and their associated tones. However, this study concentrates on examining the specific influence of assimilation on the features of segments in igiHa. ... the igiHa phonological system is structured around a systematic organization of segments (both consonants and vowels) and prosodic elements (such as syllables and tones) ... (Harjula, 2004; 2005; Bichwa and Kombe, 2017).
